text: This capstone's three lessons didn't just use this course's own seven chapters -- they pulled together all four courses of the Advanced Specialization stage, the same stage this course now closes. This final lesson reviews what each course actually contributed, and names the real stage that comes next.

Security Engineering and Identity Management is why Meridian's Conditional Access policy and identity-as-perimeter thinking needed no introduction in Lesson 29. Azure and AWS Cloud Security is why a hybrid design spanning on-prem, Azure, and AWS felt like one coherent problem instead of three separate disciplines. Python Security Automation and DevSecOps is why the containment playbook and workload identity tokens were real, automated infrastructure instead of a vague promise that an engineer would handle it manually.

Put together, the four courses of this stage form a clear progression: identity engineering, then cloud security expressed per provider, then automation that turns controls into code, then this capstone, which combines all of it into one scored, roadmapped architecture. No single course alone would have surfaced Lesson 31's gap -- it lived in the space between individually correct controls, not inside any one of them.

That's the real difference between this stage and any one course in it. A strong identity engineer writes a correct policy. A strong cloud security engineer locks down an account. A strong automation engineer writes a containment script that fires correctly. Seeing the gap between all three -- noticing what a checklist was never asked to cover -- is the architecture-level judgment this whole stage was building toward.

The Advanced Specialization stage -- Security Engineering and Identity Management, Azure and AWS Cloud Security, Python Security Automation and DevSecOps, and this Zero Trust capstone -- is complete. The next stage, Expert Specialization, is four courses that build on everything here but not on each other: Digital Forensics and Malware Analysis, Ethical Hacking and Penetration Testing and Purple Team, AI Security Engineering and Adversarial AI Defense, and Enterprise Security Architecture, GRC, and Risk Management.

Those four can be taken in any order from here, because each stands on identity, cloud security, automation, and zero trust architecture thinking rather than on one another. The Advanced Specialization stage is done. Expert Specialization starts next, with whichever of its four courses you choose first.
